newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria's last chance is sell-offs, bank closures.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria's last chance is sell-offs, bank closures.

text.p: By Elisaveta Konstantinova

Bulgaria's socialist government saw bank closures, high interest rates and speedy sell-offs to foreign investors as the last chance for the crumbling economy, but analysts said the measures were too little too late.

In a last dash to stabilise the country's wrecked financial system, Bulgaria's central bank on Monday placed nine ailing banks under special supervision and hiked the central interest rate to an all-time high of 300 percent.
"The bank had no choice other than leave few bigger banks and let the fittest survive," said Krassen Stanchev, who heads the Institute for Market Economics, an independent think-tank.
But he warned the effect of the high rate would be short-lived, and soon the central bank will have to seek new solutions.
He said it was more likely that Bulgarians will prefer to keep their savings at home in dollars rather than deposit them in unstable banks to profit from the high yield.

Payments on Bulgaria's 600 billion lev ($2.55 billion) domestic debt will become unsustainable for the budget, as a 300 percent annual interest rate entails 25 percent monthly interest payments, said a finance ministry official, who declined to be named.
The government already had to cover September's maturity payments by new issues of government securities.
Commercial banks will be unable to pay such a high interest on deposits. On Tuesday local banks were still discussing their new interest rates.

"The 300 percent interest rate can not restore confidence in the lev. Obviously the government relies on attracting speculatve capital from abroad," macroeconomic expert Mariela Nenova said in an interview with Pari daily.
But a resident foreign banker said government securities were a high risk.
"With the expected 300 interest on lev investments, the lev may devalue by up to 500 percent in the same timeframe and one will end up a looser," said the banker who declined to be named.
The lev was trading around 70 levs to dollar in January and today was trading at around 230.
"There is no reason in a shocking rise in interest rates. But there is a need for clear economic measures. The state must sell quickly without further delay," said Miteva.

In a televised address on Monday, Prime Minister Zhan Videnov announced the government's plans to sell off half a dozen major state enterprises by year-end hoping to raise around $1 billion. He has not named the companies.

Lists of possible state firms earmarked for speedy sell-offs circulated by local media included chemical giants Sodi Devnia and Chimko Vratsa, Pirdop Copper Smelter, a Devnia-based polymer producer and few cement plants among others.
Talks on the sell-off of a 25-percent stake in the Bulgarian Telecommunications Company started earlier this year.
Privatisation proceeds are expected to boost the central bank's foreign exchange reserves which will be used to stablise local banks, support the lev and cover foreign debt payments.
The sell-offs were delayed and now will yield a much lower revenue, said Stanchev.
He saw the solution in the complete liberalisation of the market, which six revolving-door governments have so far deferred.
"The only solution is to lift all price controls and so- called minimum prices on land, on government securities, on goods and restrictions on employment," said Stanchev.
Videnov's government came to power last January after the Bulgarian Socialist Party, largely composed of ex-communists, retained its grip on power in December 1994 elections.
The International Monetary Fund delayed a second $115 million tranche of funding agreed three months ago until the government completed closures for loss-making state enterprises.
In its 17-month rule the socialist government has sent mixed signals on its economic policy.
"The crisis of confidence was provoked by lack of clear intentions, uncertainty and frequent changes of the government's position. The crisis could be overcome by a political shock," said Nenova.
